projects.title: Product case study: discovery, backlog and roadmap for a real app
projects.summary: Pick an app people use every day, interview five of its users, turn what you learn into a problem statement, a prioritised backlog and a one-page roadmap, and write it up as a case study.
projects.why: Product Owner offers ask for experience you cannot get without the job. A case study on a real product shows the whole thinking recruiters test in interviews: talking to users, choosing what not to build, and explaining why.

data.name: User interviews (Nielsen Norman Group)
data.note: How to prepare an interview guide and ask about past behaviour, not wishes.

data.name: User stories (Atlassian)
data.note: The format and examples of user stories, epics and acceptance criteria.

data.name: The Scrum Guide
data.note: What the Product Owner is accountable for: product goal and backlog.

steps.title: Choose the product
steps.text: Pick an app you and people around you use often (transport, banking, food delivery, a job site). Write in three sentences who it is for and how it makes money.

steps.title: Interview five users
steps.text: Prepare 8 open questions about the last time they used it for a specific task. Record notes, not opinions: what they did, where they hesitated, what they did instead.

steps.title: Find the problem
steps.text: Group the notes on a board (Miro or paper). Write one problem statement: who, what they try to do, what blocks them, how often.

steps.title: Write the backlog
steps.text: Write 3 epics and 12 to 15 user stories with acceptance criteria that address the problem. Keep each story small enough for one sprint.

steps.title: Prioritise
steps.text: Score the stories with RICE (reach, impact, confidence, effort) in a sheet. Mark what you would not build and why.

steps.title: Roadmap and metrics
steps.text: Place the work in Now / Next / Later on one page, each block with the metric it should move.

steps.title: Write the case study
steps.text: Two pages or a short slide deck: the problem, the evidence, your choices, the roadmap and how you would measure success.

deliverables: Interview notes (anonymised) and the problem statement
The backlog with acceptance criteria and RICE scores
A one-page Now / Next / Later roadmap with metrics
A 2-page case study or 8-slide deck, linked from your CV and LinkedIn
checklist: Interview questions ask about past behaviour, not about what users would like
The problem statement names a user, a goal and an obstacle
Every story follows As a / I want / so that and has testable acceptance criteria
At least three ideas are explicitly not prioritised, with the reason
Each roadmap block has one metric with a baseline or a way to get it

cv.bullet: Led a product discovery case study on [app] (personal project): 5 user interviews, a problem statement, 15 user stories prioritised with RICE and an outcome-based roadmap.
cv.talk: Explain the most surprising thing users told you, how it changed your backlog, and one feature you chose not to build.

stretch: Make a clickable Figma mock-up of the top story and test it with two of the users.
Estimate the RICE reach with public data (app store downloads, reviews).
Write the release note for the first story as if it shipped.

projects.title: A product backlog and two sprints in Jira
projects.summary: Set up a free Jira project for a small product idea, write and refine the backlog, plan and run two one-week sprints with friends or alone, and share the board, the sprint reports and a short retrospective.
projects.why: Almost every Product Owner offer names Jira and Scrum. A real board with refined stories, sprint goals and reports shows you can do the daily work, not only talk about it.

data.name: Jira Free
data.note: The free plan for up to 10 users: enough for a portfolio project.

data.name: The Scrum Guide
data.note: Sprint planning, review and retrospective: what each event is for.

data.name: User stories (Atlassian)
data.note: Examples of stories, epics and acceptance criteria.

steps.title: Pick a small product
steps.text: A to-do app for students, a club website, a recipe planner: something you can describe in one sentence.

steps.title: Create the project
steps.text: Create a Scrum project in Jira, add the product goal to the board description, and create 3 epics.

steps.title: Write and refine the backlog
steps.text: Write 15 stories with acceptance criteria and story points; split any story bigger than 5 points.

steps.title: Sprint 1
steps.text: Write a sprint goal, pull the stories that serve it, run the sprint (build, mock or simulate the work) and keep the board up to date.

steps.title: Review and retrospective
steps.text: Write what was done against the goal, what you learned, and two improvements for the next sprint.

steps.title: Sprint 2
steps.text: Re-order the backlog from what you learned, run the second sprint and compare the two sprint reports.

steps.title: Share it
steps.text: Take screenshots of the board, the backlog and the sprint reports, and write a one-page summary.

deliverables: The Jira board and backlog (screenshots or a public link)
Two sprint goals and sprint reports
A one-page summary linked from your CV
checklist: The product goal is written on the board
Every story has acceptance criteria and an estimate
No story is bigger than the team can finish in one sprint
Each sprint has a goal that is not just a list of tickets
The backlog order changed after sprint 1, with the reason written down
Retrospective actions are specific and have an owner

cv.bullet: Ran two Scrum sprints on [product] in Jira (personal project): product goal, 15 refined user stories with acceptance criteria, sprint goals, reviews and retrospectives.
cv.talk: Walk through how you split one big story, and what you changed in the backlog after the first sprint review.

stretch: Add a Kanban board for bugs and compare the two ways of working.
Write a Definition of Done and check each story against it.
Invite two friends as stakeholders and run a real sprint review.

projects.title: Measure a product: funnel and A/B test analysis
projects.summary: Use the Google Analytics demo account of a real online store to define product metrics, build a purchase funnel, find where users drop out, and design an A/B test with its sample size and success criteria.
projects.why: Product Owners are expected to make decisions with data. This project shows you can choose metrics, read a funnel and set up an experiment properly, which is exactly what interviews test with case questions.

data.name: Google Analytics demo account
data.note: Real, anonymised data of the Google Merchandise Store, free with a Google account.

data.name: A/B test sample size calculator
data.note: How many users each variant needs before the result means something.

data.name: Intro to SQL (Kaggle Learn)
data.note: Enough SQL to query event data yourself if you go further with BigQuery.

steps.title: Set a goal
steps.text: Write one product goal for the store as an OKR: an objective and two or three measurable key results.

steps.title: Explore the data
steps.text: Open the GA4 demo account; note users, sessions, conversion rate and revenue for the last 3 months.

steps.title: Build the funnel
steps.text: Use an exploration to build a funnel: view product, add to cart, begin checkout, purchase. Note the drop at each step by device.

steps.title: Find the biggest leak
steps.text: Pick the step with the biggest drop and write three hypotheses about why users leave there.

steps.title: Design an A/B test
steps.text: Choose one hypothesis, describe the change, the primary metric and a guardrail metric, and compute the sample size and duration.

steps.title: Write the decision rule
steps.text: Before any result, write what you would do if the test wins, loses or shows no difference.

steps.title: Write it up
steps.text: A two-page analysis with the funnel chart, the hypotheses, the test design and the decision rule.

deliverables: The funnel chart with drop-off rates by device
The A/B test design: hypothesis, metrics, sample size, duration, decision rule
A 2-page analysis linked from your CV
checklist: Key results are measurable and have a target
The funnel uses the same date range for every step
Hypotheses are about user behaviour, not about the tool
The test has one primary metric and at least one guardrail
Sample size uses a realistic baseline and minimum detectable effect from the data
The decision rule is written before looking at any result

cv.bullet: Analysed the purchase funnel of an online store in Google Analytics 4 (personal project): defined OKRs, found the biggest drop-off and designed an A/B test with sample size and decision rules.
cv.talk: Explain why you chose your primary and guardrail metrics, and what you would do if the test showed no significant difference.

stretch: Query the public GA4 sample in BigQuery with SQL to rebuild the funnel yourself.
Segment the funnel by new and returning users.
Write the user story and acceptance criteria for the change you would test.
